reminder: A least fixed point is a [fixed point](c:fixed-point) that lies below every other fixed point.
definition: Let $f:P\to P$ be a map on a set $P$ with a [partial order](c:partial-order). A least fixed point of $f$ is an element $x$ with $f(x)=x$ and $x\le y$ for every $y$ with $f(y)=y$.
examples: For $f(x)=x^2$ on $[0,1]$ the fixed points are $0$ and $1$, and $0$ is the least fixed point.
A [monotone](c:monotone-function) map $f$ on a [complete lattice](c:complete-lattice) has the least fixed point $\bigwedge\{x : f(x)\le x\}$ (Knaster-Tarski).

Kleene: if $f$ is [Scott-continuous](c:scott-continuity) on a [directed-complete partial order](c:dcpo) with least element $\bot$, the least fixed point is the supremum of $\bot, f(\bot), f(f(\bot)),\dots$.
Non-example: for $f(x)=x$ on $[0,1]$ every point is fixed, and $\tfrac12$ is not the least fixed point, because $0$ is also fixed and $0<\tfrac12$.

steps: Start with any [fixed point](c:fixed-point) $x$ of $f$, so $f(x)=x$.
Compare $x$ with every other fixed point $y$ in the [partial order](c:partial-order).
Require $x\le y$ for all fixed points $y$.
Then $x$ is the least fixed point, and it is unique if it exists.
links.why: It shows the one condition that picks a canonical fixed point out of all fixed points.

reminder: A least squares solution makes the sum of the squared errors as small as possible.
definition: For a [matrix](c:matrix) $A$ and a vector $b$, a least squares solution of $Ax=b$ is a vector $\hat x$ that minimizes the squared [Euclidean distance](c:euclidean-distance) $\|b-Ax\|^2$. Equivalently, $A\hat x$ is the [orthogonal projection](c:orthogonal-projection) of $b$ onto the column space of $A$, and $A^{T}A\hat x=A^{T}b$.
examples: To fit a line $y=a+bx$ to points $(x_i,y_i)$, choose $a,b$ to minimize $\sum_i (y_i-a-bx_i)^2$.
If $Ax=b$ has an exact solution, that solution is a least squares solution with error zero.
The mean of numbers $y_1,\dots,y_n$ is the least squares fit by a constant, because it minimizes $\sum_i (y_i-c)^2$.
Non-example: minimizing $\sum_i |y_i-a-bx_i|$ gives a least absolute deviations fit, not a least squares fit.

reminder: A Lie algebra-valued form is a [differential form](c:differential-form) whose values lie in a fixed [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra).
definition: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) and $M$ a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold). A $\mathfrak g$-valued $k$-form on $M$ is a smooth section of $\Lambda^k T^*M\otimes\mathfrak g$, that is, a [differential form](c:differential-form) of degree $k$ with values in $\mathfrak g$. In a basis $e_a$ of $\mathfrak g$ it is a sum $\sum_a\omega^a e_a$ of ordinary $k$-forms, and the bracket of $\mathfrak g$ gives a product $[\alpha\wedge\beta]$ of such forms.
examples: A local connection form of a principal $G$-bundle is a $\mathfrak g$-valued $1$-form on the base.
The [Maurer-Cartan form](c:maurer-cartan-form) $\theta=g^{-1}dg$ on a Lie group $G$ is a $\mathfrak g$-valued $1$-form.
For $\mathfrak g=\mathbb R$ the $\mathfrak g$-valued forms are the ordinary real differential forms.
Non-example: a smooth map $g:M\to G$ into the group is not a $\mathfrak g$-valued $0$-form, but its logarithmic derivative $g^{-1}dg$ is a $\mathfrak g$-valued $1$-form.

steps: Take the [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak g=\mathbb R$ with zero bracket.
A $\mathfrak g$-valued $k$-form is then a section of $\Lambda^kT^*M\otimes\mathbb R=\Lambda^kT^*M$.
So it is an ordinary real [differential form](c:differential-form) of degree $k$.
links.why: It lets a learner reuse everything known about ordinary forms; only the bracket of the values is new.

reminder: A Lie superalgebra is a $\mathbb Z_2$-graded vector space with a graded-antisymmetric bracket that satisfies a graded Jacobi identity.
definition: A Lie superalgebra is a [super vector space](c:super-vector-space) $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak g_0\oplus\mathfrak g_1$ with a bilinear bracket of degree $0$ such that $[x,y]=-(-1)^{|x||y|}[y,x]$ and $[x,[y,z]]=[[x,y],z]+(-1)^{|x||y|}[y,[x,z]]$ for homogeneous $x,y,z$. Then $\mathfrak g_0$ is an ordinary [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) and $\mathfrak g_1$ is a representation of it.
examples: The endomorphisms of $\mathbb C^{m|n}$ with the supercommutator $[A,B]=AB-(-1)^{|A||B|}BA$ form the Lie superalgebra $\mathfrak{gl}(m|n)$.
Every ordinary Lie algebra is a Lie superalgebra with $\mathfrak g_1=0$.
The super Poincaré algebra has the Poincaré algebra as its even part and the supercharges $Q$ as its odd part, with $[Q,Q]$ equal to a translation.
Non-example: the plain commutator $AB-BA$ on $\mathfrak{gl}(1|1)$ is not a Lie superalgebra bracket, because for odd $A,B$ it is antisymmetric where the rule asks for symmetric.

steps: Take a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak g$ and put $\mathfrak g_0=\mathfrak g$ and $\mathfrak g_1=0$.
Every element is even, so each sign $(-1)^{|x||y|}$ equals $1$.
The super rules then reduce to antisymmetry and the ordinary Jacobi identity.
links.why: It shows that a Lie superalgebra with no odd part is exactly a Lie algebra, so Lie algebra facts are the even part of the super case.

reminder: A limit cycle is a closed orbit that another trajectory approaches in forward or backward time.
definition: A limit cycle of a [dynamical system](c:dynamical-system), for example of a planar [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $\dot x=f(x)$, is a [periodic orbit](c:periodic-orbit) $\Gamma$ that is the [limit set](c:limit-set) of some trajectory not in $\Gamma$. In the plane this forces $\Gamma$ to be isolated: no other closed orbit lies close to it.
examples: The van der Pol oscillator $\ddot x-\mu(1-x^2)\dot x+x=0$ with $\mu>0$ has exactly one limit cycle, and it is stable.
For $\dot r=r(1-r^2)$, $\dot\theta=1$ the unit circle is a stable limit cycle, because every orbit that starts off the origin spirals toward it.
Non-example: the circles of the harmonic oscillator $\ddot x+x=0$ are closed orbits but not limit cycles, because nearby orbits are also closed and none approaches them.

steps: Take a limit cycle $\Gamma$; by definition it is a [periodic orbit](c:periodic-orbit).
Add the condition that some trajectory outside $\Gamma$ has $\Gamma$ as its limit set.
Periodic orbits with no such nearby trajectory, as in the harmonic oscillator, are left out.
links.why: It shows that a limit cycle is a periodic orbit that also attracts or repels its neighbors.

steps: Take a limit cycle $\Gamma$ and a trajectory $\gamma$ outside $\Gamma$ whose limit set is $\Gamma$.
Then $\Gamma$ is the [limit set](c:limit-set) of $\gamma$, by definition.
The special case adds that this limit set is a single closed orbit.
links.why: It shows that a limit cycle is the simplest kind of limit set, apart from an equilibrium.

reminder: The limit set of a trajectory is the set of points that the trajectory comes arbitrarily close to at arbitrarily late times.
definition: Let $\varphi_t$ be a [flow](c:flow) on a [metric space](c:metric-space) $X$ and let $p\in X$. The ($\omega$-)limit set $\omega(p)$ is the set of points $q$ for which some sequence $t_n\to+\infty$ has $\varphi_{t_n}(p)\to q$, and the $\alpha$-limit set uses $t_n\to-\infty$.
examples: If $p$ is an equilibrium, then $\omega(p)=\{p\}$.
If the orbit of $p$ spirals toward a closed orbit $\Gamma$, then $\omega(p)=\Gamma$.
For $\dot x=-x$ on $\mathbb R$ every point $p$ has $\omega(p)=\{0\}$.
Non-example: for $\dot x=-x$ and $p=1$ the orbit $\{e^{-t}\}$ is not the limit set, because $\omega(p)=\{0\}$ and $0$ is not on the orbit.

steps: Start with a [limit set](c:limit-set) $\omega(p)$ of a trajectory.
Require that $\omega(p)$ is one [periodic orbit](c:periodic-orbit) $\Gamma$.
Require also that $p$ does not lie on $\Gamma$.
Then $\Gamma$ is a limit cycle.
links.why: It shows what a limit cycle adds to a limit set: a closed orbit approached by a trajectory off the orbit.

reminder: The limit superior of a sequence is the largest limit of any of its subsequences.
definition: For a [sequence](c:sequence) $(a_n)$ of [real numbers](c:real-number), $\limsup a_n=\inf_n s_n$, where $s_n=\sup_{k\ge n}a_k$ is the [least upper bound](c:least-upper-bound) of the tail from $n$ on; the value may be $\pm\infty$. For sets $A_n$, $\limsup A_n=\bigcap_n\bigcup_{k\ge n}A_k$ is the set of points that lie in infinitely many $A_n$.
examples: The sequence $a_n=(-1)^n(1+\tfrac1n)$ has $\limsup a_n=1$ and has no limit.
For events $A_n$ in a probability space, $\limsup A_n$ is the event that infinitely many $A_n$ occur (Borel-Cantelli lemmas).
By the Cauchy-Hadamard theorem the radius of convergence of $\sum c_nz^n$ is $1/\limsup|c_n|^{1/n}$.
Non-example: $\sup_n a_n$ is not $\limsup a_n$; for $a_n=1/n$ we get $\sup_n a_n=1$ but $\limsup a_n=0$.

steps: Take a sequence with $a_n\to L$; the tail suprema $s_n=\sup_{k\ge n}a_k$ form a non-increasing sequence.
For $\varepsilon>0$ all $a_k$ with $k\ge n$ lie within $\varepsilon$ of $L$ once $n$ is large, so $|s_n-L|\le\varepsilon$.
A non-increasing sequence has $\inf_n s_n=\lim_n s_n$, so $\limsup a_n=L$.
The limit superior also exists when the sequence has no [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence).
links.why: It shows that the limit superior agrees with the limit whenever the limit exists, and still gives an answer when it does not.

reminder: A Lindelöf space is a space in which every [open cover](c:open-cover) has a countable subcover.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is Lindelöf if every [open cover](c:open-cover) of $X$ has a subfamily that still covers $X$ and is [countable](c:countable-set).
examples: Every compact space is Lindelöf, because a finite subcover is countable.
Every [second-countable space](c:second-countable-space) is Lindelöf, so $\mathbb R^n$ is Lindelöf.
The Sorgenfrey line is Lindelöf, although it is not second-countable.
Non-example: an uncountable discrete space is not Lindelöf, because the cover by singletons has no countable subcover.

steps: Take a [compact space](c:compact-space) $X$ and an open cover of $X$.
Compactness gives a finite subcover.
A finite family is countable, so the subcover is countable.
Hence $X$ is Lindelöf.
links.why: It shows that Lindelöf asks for less than compactness: a countable subcover instead of a finite one.

steps: Take a countable base $\{B_n\}$ of $X$ and an open cover $\mathcal U$ of $X$.
For each $n$ such that $B_n$ lies inside some member of $\mathcal U$, pick one such member $U_n$.
A point $x$ lies in some $U\in\mathcal U$, hence in some $B_n\subseteq U$, hence in $U_n$.
So the countably many sets $U_n$ cover $X$.
links.why: It shows why every second-countable space is Lindelöf (Lindelöf's lemma).

reminder: A line is a straight, unbounded, one-dimensional figure, and any two distinct points lie on exactly one line.
definition: In a [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space), a line is a set $\{p+tv : t\in\mathbb R\}$ for a [point](c:point) $p$ and a nonzero direction vector $v$. It is a one-dimensional [affine subspace](c:affine-subspace): the line through $p$ with direction $v$.
examples: In the plane, the solutions of $ax+by=c$ with $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$ form a line.
In $\mathbb R^3$ the set $\{(1,0,0)+t(0,1,1) : t\in\mathbb R\}$ is a line.
Non-example: a circle is not a line, because it is curved and no single direction vector $v$ describes it.
Non-example: a line segment is not a line, because it is bounded and the parameter $t$ does not range over all of $\mathbb R$.

steps: An [affine subspace](c:affine-subspace) has the form $p+W$ for a point $p$ and a linear subspace $W$.
Take $W$ of dimension one, so $W=\{tv\}$ for a nonzero vector $v$.
Then $p+W$ is the line through $p$ with direction $v$.
links.why: It shows that a line is the one-dimensional case; planes and hyperplanes are the next cases.

reminder: A line arrangement is a finite set of distinct [lines](c:line) in a plane.
definition: A line arrangement is a finite set $\mathcal L$ of distinct [lines](c:line) in the [plane](c:plane), affine or [projective](c:projective-plane). Its vertices are the points that lie on two or more of the lines, and the lines cut the plane into edges and faces.
examples: Three lines, no two parallel and not meeting in one point, give $3$ vertices and $7$ faces in the real plane.
The $n$ lines through one point give one vertex and $2n$ faces.
The lines that join pairs of $n$ given points form a line arrangement; Beck's theorem bounds how many distinct lines it has.
Non-example: the lines $y=n$ for all integers $n$ form an infinite family, so they are not a line arrangement.

steps: A hyperplane in a space of dimension $d$ is an affine subspace of dimension $d-1$.
Take $d=2$; the hyperplanes of the plane are exactly the [lines](c:line).
A finite set of such hyperplanes is an arrangement, so a finite set of lines is a line arrangement.
links.why: It lets a learner use facts about arrangements of hyperplanes in the planar case.

reminder: A linear algebraic group is a Zariski-closed subgroup of a general linear group over a field.
definition: Let $k$ be a [field](c:field). A linear algebraic group over $k$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $G$ of the [general linear group](c:general-linear-group) $GL_n(k)$, for some $n$, that is closed in the [Zariski topology](c:zariski-topology), that is, cut out by polynomial equations in the matrix entries. Equivalently, it is an affine [algebraic group](c:algebraic-group).
examples: $SL_n$, the orthogonal group $O_n$ and the group of invertible upper triangular matrices are closed subgroups of $GL_n$ given by polynomial equations.
The multiplicative group $\mathbb G_m=GL_1$ is linear, and so is the additive group $\mathbb G_a$, which is the group of matrices $\begin{pmatrix}1&x\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
Non-example: $SL_2(\mathbb Z)$ is a subgroup of $GL_2(\mathbb C)$ but is not Zariski closed, because its Zariski closure is $SL_2(\mathbb C)$.
Non-example: an elliptic curve over $\mathbb C$ is an algebraic group, but it is projective and has no closed embedding into a matrix group.

steps: An [algebraic group](c:algebraic-group) is a variety with group operations that are algebraic maps.
A closed subgroup $G\subseteq GL_n$ is an affine variety, and multiplication and inversion are polynomial maps in the entries.
So $G$ is an algebraic group, and the special case adds that $G$ is affine.
links.why: It shows that linear algebraic groups are the affine algebraic groups, so they are the matrix-group part of algebraic group theory.

reminder: A linear differential operator is a [linear map](c:linear-map) that sends a function to a combination of its derivatives.
definition: A linear differential operator of order $m$ on functions of $x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ is a map $L=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}a_\alpha(x)\,\partial^\alpha$, where each $a_\alpha$ is a [function](c:function) and $\partial^\alpha$ is a [partial derivative](c:partial-derivative) of order $|\alpha|$. It is a [linear map](c:linear-map): $L(cf+g)=c\,Lf+Lg$ for constants $c$.
examples: The [Laplace operator](c:laplace-operator) $\Delta=\sum_i\partial_i^2$ is a linear differential operator of order $2$.
The operator $L=\frac{d}{dx}+x$ acts by $Lf=f'+xf$ and has order $1$.
Every linear ordinary differential equation $y^{(m)}+a_{m-1}(x)y^{(m-1)}+\dots+a_0(x)y=g$ has the form $Ly=g$ for such an operator $L$.
Non-example: $f\mapsto (f')^2$ is not linear, because $(f'+g')^2\ne (f')^2+(g')^2$ in general.

steps: Take the space of smooth functions and the maps $Lf=\sum_\alpha a_\alpha\,\partial^\alpha f$ with finitely many terms.
Each partial derivative is a [linear map](c:linear-map), and so is multiplication by a fixed function $a_\alpha$.
A finite sum of linear maps is linear, so $L$ is a linear map with the extra form of a differential operator.
links.why: It shows that results about linear maps, such as superposition of solutions, apply to differential operators.

reminder: A linear group is a [group](c:group) with an injective homomorphism into a general linear group over a field.
definition: A [group](c:group) $G$ is linear if there are a [field](c:field) $k$ and an integer $n\ge1$ with an injective homomorphism $G\to GL_n(k)$ into the [general linear group](c:general-linear-group). Equivalently, $G$ has a [faithful representation](c:faithful-representation) on a [finite-dimensional vector space](c:finite-dimensional-vector-space) over $k$.
examples: Every finite group is linear, by permutation matrices.
The groups $SL_n(\mathbb Z)$ and the free group $F_2$ are linear; $F_2$ embeds in $SL_2(\mathbb Z)$.
Every compact Lie group is linear, by the Peter-Weyl theorem.
Non-example: the universal cover of $SL_2(\mathbb R)$ has no faithful finite-dimensional representation, so it is not a linear group.

steps: Take a [finite group](c:finite-group) $G$ with $n$ elements.
Let $G$ permute its own elements by left multiplication; this is an injective homomorphism $G\to S_n$.
Send each permutation to its permutation matrix in $GL_n(k)$ for any field $k$.
The composite $G\to GL_n(k)$ is injective, so $G$ is linear.
links.why: It shows that every result about linear groups, such as the Jordan-Schur theorem, covers all finite groups.

reminder: Linear programming maximizes or minimizes a linear function over the points that satisfy linear inequalities.
definition: A linear program is an optimization problem: maximize $c^{T}x$ over $x\in\mathbb R^n$ subject to $Ax\le b$ and $x\ge0$, for a given [matrix](c:matrix) $A$ and vectors $b,c$. The feasible set is a [convex polyhedron](c:convex-polyhedron), and the objective $x\mapsto c^{T}x$ is a [linear functional](c:linear-functional).
examples: Maximize $3x+2y$ subject to $x+y\le4$, $x\le2$ and $x,y\ge0$; the optimum is at $(2,2)$ with value $10$.
The maximum flow problem in a network is a linear program in the flow variables, with the capacities as constraints.
A diet problem chooses food amounts at least cost so that each nutrient reaches its minimum; it is a linear program.
Non-example: minimizing $x^2$ subject to $x\ge1$ is not a linear program, because the objective $x^2$ is not linear.

reminder: Every [linear program](c:linear-programming) has a dual program, and their optimal values are equal when an optimum exists.
definition: To the [linear program](c:linear-programming) $\max\{c^{T}x : Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}$ belongs the dual program $\min\{b^{T}y : A^{T}y\ge c,\ y\ge0\}$. Weak duality says $c^{T}x\le b^{T}y$ for all feasible $x$ and $y$; strong duality says the two optimal values are equal when one of the programs has a finite optimum.
examples: The program $\max x$ subject to $x\le3$, $x\ge0$ has the dual $\min 3y$ subject to $y\ge1$, $y\ge0$, and both have value $3$.
The dual of the maximum flow program is a fractional minimum cut program, which gives the Max-flow min-cut theorem.
In a zero-sum game the optimal mixed strategies of the two players solve a pair of dual programs, which gives the minimax theorem.
Non-example: for an integer program the equality can fail, because its optimum can lie strictly below the common value of the relaxation and the dual.

reminder: A linear recurrence defines each term of a [sequence](c:sequence) as a fixed linear combination of the terms just before it.
definition: A linear recurrence of order $n$ over a [commutative semiring](c:comm-semiring) $R$ is given by coefficients $a_0,\dots,a_{n-1}\in R$. A [sequence](c:sequence) $u:\mathbb N\to R$ satisfies it when $u(k+n)=\sum_{i<n}a_i\,u(k+i)$ for every $k$.
examples: The [Fibonacci numbers](c:fibonacci-numbers) satisfy $u(k+2)=u(k+1)+u(k)$, a recurrence of order $2$ with coefficients $1,1$.
A geometric sequence satisfies $u(k+1)=r\,u(k)$, a recurrence of order $1$.
The squares $u(k)=k^2$ satisfy $u(k+3)=3u(k+2)-3u(k+1)+u(k)$, a recurrence of order $3$.
Non-example: $u(k+1)=u(k)^2$ is not linear in the previous term, and $u(k+1)=(k+1)\,u(k)$ has a coefficient that depends on $k$, so neither is a linear recurrence with fixed coefficients.

reminder: Linear regression models a response as a linear function of explanatory variables plus a random error.
definition: In linear regression one models a response vector $y$ as $y=X\beta+\varepsilon$, where $X$ is a known [matrix](c:matrix) of explanatory variables, $\beta$ is a vector of unknown coefficients and $\varepsilon$ is a vector of errors that are [random variables](c:random-variable). The coefficients are usually estimated by [least squares](c:least-squares), which chooses $\beta$ to minimize $\|y-X\beta\|^2$.
examples: Simple linear regression fits $y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i$ to pairs $(x_i,y_i)$.
Polynomial regression $y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2+\varepsilon$ is still linear regression, because the model is linear in the coefficients $\beta$.
By the Gauss-Markov theorem, if the errors are uncorrelated with equal variance, least squares gives the best linear unbiased estimator of $\beta$.
Non-example: $y=\beta_0e^{\beta_1x}+\varepsilon$ is not linear regression, because the model is not linear in $\beta_1$.

reminder: A map has linearity when it preserves sums and scalar multiples.
definition: A map $f$ between [vector spaces](c:vector-space) over a field $k$ is linear when $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ and $f(cx)=c\,f(x)$ for all vectors $x,y$ and all scalars $c$. Equivalently, $f(ax+by)=a\,f(x)+b\,f(y)$, and such a map is a [linear map](c:linear-map).
examples: Differentiation $f\mapsto f'$ on smooth functions is linear, because $(af+bg)'=af'+bg'$.
Every matrix $A$ gives a linear map $x\mapsto Ax$.
The time evolution of a closed quantum system is linear, and the proof of the no-cloning theorem uses this.
Non-example: $f(x)=x+1$ on $\mathbb R$ is not linear, because $f(0)=1\ne0$, and $f(x)=x^2$ is not linear, because $(1+1)^2\ne1^2+1^2$.

steps: An [addition-preserving map](c:add-hom) satisfies $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$.
Take such a map between vector spaces over $k$.
Add the condition $f(cx)=c\,f(x)$ for every scalar $c$.
Then $f$ is linear.
links.why: It shows that linearity is additivity plus compatibility with scalars.

reminder: Linearization replaces a smooth map or system near a point by its best linear approximation there.
definition: The linearization of a smooth map $f$ at a point $p$ is the linear map given by the [derivative](c:derivative) $Df(p)$, the [Jacobian matrix](c:jacobian-matrix), so that $f(p+h)\approx f(p)+Df(p)\,h$. For an [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $\dot x=f(x)$ with an equilibrium $p$, the linearized system is $\dot y=Df(p)\,y$ with $y=x-p$.
examples: The pendulum equation $\ddot\theta=-\sin\theta$ linearizes at $\theta=0$ to $\ddot\theta=-\theta$.
For $\dot x=x-x^3$ at $x=0$ the linearization is $\dot y=y$, which grows, so $0$ is unstable.
By the Hartman-Grobman theorem, near a hyperbolic equilibrium the flow is topologically conjugate to the flow of its linearization.
Non-example: the second-order Taylor polynomial $f(p)+Df(p)h+\tfrac12D^2f(p)(h,h)$ is not a linearization, because it is not linear in $h$.

reminder: A local field is a non-discrete locally compact Hausdorff topological field.
definition: A local field is a [topological field](c:topological-field) whose topology is [locally compact](c:locally-compact-space), [Hausdorff](c:hausdorff-space) and not discrete. Up to isomorphism the local fields are $\mathbb R$, $\mathbb C$, the finite extensions of the [field of p-adic numbers](c:p-adic-number) $\mathbb Q_p$, and the fields $\mathbb F_q((t))$ of [Laurent series](c:laurent-series) over a finite field; some authors keep only the non-archimedean ones.
examples: $\mathbb Q_p$ is a local field; the ring $\mathbb Z_p$ is a compact open neighborhood of $0$.
$\mathbb F_p((t))$ is a local field of characteristic $p$.
$\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb C$ are the archimedean local fields.
Non-example: $\mathbb Q$ with the usual topology is not locally compact, because no compact set contains an open interval around a point.

steps: A [topological field](c:topological-field) is a field whose topology makes addition, multiplication and inversion continuous.
Take such a field.
Add three conditions: the topology is locally compact, Hausdorff and not discrete.
The result is a local field.
links.why: It shows that a local field is a topological field with enough compactness to carry a Haar measure, which is what number theory uses.

reminder: In a locally compact space every point has a neighborhood basis of compact sets.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is locally compact if every point $x$ has a basis of [compact](c:compact-space) [neighborhoods](c:neighborhood): each neighborhood of $x$ contains a compact neighborhood of $x$. For [Hausdorff spaces](c:hausdorff-space) this is equivalent to having one compact neighborhood at each point, and many authors use that weaker condition as the definition.
examples: $\mathbb R^n$ is locally compact, because closed balls are compact neighborhoods.
Every discrete space and every compact Hausdorff space is locally compact.
Every open subset and every closed subset of a locally compact Hausdorff space is locally compact.
Non-example: an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is not locally compact, because no closed ball in it is compact.

steps: Take a [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space) $X$ and a point $x$.
A compact Hausdorff space is regular, so the closed neighborhoods of $x$ form a neighborhood basis.
A closed subset of a compact space is compact, so those closed neighborhoods are compact.
So $x$ has a basis of compact neighborhoods, and $X$ is locally compact.
links.why: It shows that every result for locally compact spaces, such as the Riesz-Markov-Kakutani theorem, also holds for compact Hausdorff spaces.

reminder: A function is log-convex when it is positive and its [logarithm](c:logarithm) is convex.
definition: A function $f:I\to(0,\infty)$ on an interval $I$ is log-convex if the [logarithm](c:logarithm) of $f$ is a [convex function](c:convex-function). Equivalently, $f(tx+(1-t)y)\le f(x)^t\,f(y)^{1-t}$ for all $x,y\in I$ and $t\in[0,1]$.
examples: $f(x)=e^{x^2}$ is log-convex, because $\log f(x)=x^2$ is convex.
The [Gamma function](c:gamma-function) is log-convex on $(0,\infty)$, and the Bohr-Mollerup theorem uses this to single it out.
$f(x)=1/x$ on $(0,\infty)$ is log-convex, because $\log f(x)=-\log x$ is convex.
Non-example: $f(x)=x$ on $(0,\infty)$ is not log-convex, because $\log x$ is concave.

steps: Take a log-convex function $f$, so $g=\log f$ is convex.
The exponential function is convex and increasing.
A convex increasing function of a convex function is convex, so $f=e^{g}$ is convex.
So every log-convex function is a [convex function](c:convex-function), and the extra condition is the convexity of $\log f$.
links.why: It shows that log-convexity is a stronger condition than convexity, so convex-function tools apply.

reminder: A positive sequence is log-convex when each term is at most the geometric mean of its two neighbors.
definition: A [sequence](c:sequence) $(a_n)_{n\ge0}$ of positive [real numbers](c:real-number) is log-convex if $a_n^2\le a_{n-1}a_{n+1}$ for all $n\ge1$. Equivalently, the [logarithms](c:logarithm) $\log a_n$ form a convex sequence, which means that their second differences are non-negative.
examples: $a_n=r^n$ with $r>0$ is log-convex, with equality $a_n^2=a_{n-1}a_{n+1}$.
$a_n=n!$ is log-convex, because $(n!)^2\le(n-1)!\,(n+1)!$ is the same as $n\le n+1$.
Quasi-analytic function classes are defined by a log-convex sequence $M_n$ of bounds on the derivatives.
Non-example: $a_n=1/n!$ is not log-convex, because the inequality would need $n+1\le n$.

steps: [Log-convexity](c:log-convexity) asks that $\log f$ be convex for a positive function $f$ on a parameter set.
Take the parameter set to be the non-negative integers, so $f$ is a sequence $a_n$.
Convexity of $\log a_n$ on the integers means $\log a_n\le\tfrac12(\log a_{n-1}+\log a_{n+1})$.
Exponentiating gives $a_n^2\le a_{n-1}a_{n+1}$.
links.why: It shows that the sequence condition is the discrete form of the same idea that holds for functions.

reminder: A positive quantity is log-convex when its [logarithm](c:logarithm) is a convex function of its parameter.
definition: A positive function $f$ on an interval, or a positive sequence on the integers, is log-convex when $\log f$ is convex, that is, $f(tx+(1-t)y)\le f(x)^t\,f(y)^{1-t}$ for $t\in[0,1]$. Log-convexity is stronger than ordinary [convexity](c:convex-function) of $f$, and it is preserved by sums, products and positive pointwise limits.
examples: Hadamard three-lines theorem: for a bounded holomorphic $f$ on a strip, $M(x)=\sup_y|f(x+iy)|$ is log-convex in $x$.
Hadamard three-circles theorem: $\log M(r)$ is a convex function of $\log r$, where $M(r)=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|$.
The moment function $s\mapsto\int x^s\,d\mu(x)$ of a positive measure is log-convex in $s$, by Hölder's inequality.
Non-example: $f(x)=x$ on $(0,\infty)$ is not log-convex, because $\log x$ is concave.

steps: Fix the parameter set to be an interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$.
Then log-convexity of $f:I\to(0,\infty)$ says that $\log f$ is convex on $I$.
That is the definition of a [log-convex function](c:log-convex-function).
links.why: It names the property once, so the function case and the sequence case are seen as one idea.

steps: Fix the parameter set to be the non-negative integers.
Then log-convexity of $a_n>0$ says that $\log a_n$ has non-negative second differences.
That is the same as $a_n^2\le a_{n-1}a_{n+1}$, the definition of a [log-convex sequence](c:log-convex-sequence).
links.why: It shows the sequence inequality as the discrete form of log-convexity.

reminder: A positive function on a lattice is log-supermodular when $f(x\vee y)f(x\wedge y)\ge f(x)f(y)$.
definition: Let $L$ be a [distributive lattice](c:distributive-lattice) with join $\vee$ and meet $\wedge$. A function $f:L\to[0,\infty)$ is log-supermodular if $f(x\vee y)\,f(x\wedge y)\ge f(x)\,f(y)$ for all $x,y\in L$. For $f>0$ this says that $\log f$ is a [supermodular function](c:supermodular-function).
examples: On $\{0,1\}^n$ with the coordinatewise order, a product weight $\mu(x)=\prod_ip_i(x_i)$ is log-supermodular, and the inequality is an equality.
The ferromagnetic Ising weight $\exp(\sum J_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j)$ with all $J_{ij}\ge0$ is log-supermodular on $\{-1,1\}^n$, which is the condition of the FKG inequality.
Non-example: $f(\sigma)=e^{J\sigma_1\sigma_2}$ with $J<0$ on $\{-1,1\}^2$ is not log-supermodular, because $x=(1,-1)$ and $y=(-1,1)$ give $e^{2J}<e^{-2J}$.

reminder: The loop group of a [Lie group](c:lie-group) is the group of smooth loops in it under pointwise multiplication.
definition: For a [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$, the loop group $LG$ is the set of [smooth maps](c:smooth-function) $\gamma:S^1\to G$ from the [circle](c:circle), with the product $(\gamma\delta)(\theta)=\gamma(\theta)\delta(\theta)$. It is itself an infinite-dimensional Lie group, and $G$ sits inside it as the constant loops.
examples: $LU(1)$ is the group of smooth maps $S^1\to U(1)$ under pointwise product, and its connected components are labeled by the winding number in $\mathbb Z$.
$LSU(2)$ is connected, because $SU(2)$ is simply connected.
The based loop group $\Omega G$ of loops with $\gamma(1)=e$ is a subgroup of $LG$, and $LG=\Omega G\rtimes G$.
Non-example: the free loop space of a space with no group structure has no pointwise product, so it is not a loop group.

reminder: A set-valued map is lower hemicontinuous when the set of points whose image meets any open set is open.
definition: Let $\Phi:X\rightrightarrows Y$ be a set-valued map between [topological spaces](c:topological-space), so $\Phi(x)\subseteq Y$ for each $x$. The map $\Phi$ is lower hemicontinuous at $x$ if for every [open set](c:open-set) $V\subseteq Y$ with $\Phi(x)\cap V\ne\emptyset$ there is a [neighborhood](c:neighborhood) $U$ of $x$ with $\Phi(x')\cap V\ne\emptyset$ for all $x'\in U$, and it is lower hemicontinuous if this holds at every point.
examples: $\Phi(x)=[-1,1]$ for $x\ne0$ and $\Phi(0)=\{0\}$ is lower hemicontinuous at $0$ (but not upper hemicontinuous), because every open set that meets $\{0\}$ also meets $[-1,1]$.
Michael's selection theorem produces a continuous selection from a lower hemicontinuous map with closed convex values.
Non-example: $\Phi(x)=\{0\}$ for $x\ne0$ and $\Phi(0)=[-1,1]$ is not lower hemicontinuous at $0$, because the open set $V=(\tfrac12,1)$ meets $\Phi(0)$ but misses $\Phi(x)$ for $x\ne0$.

steps: Take a function $f:X\to Y$ and view it as the set-valued map $\Phi(x)=\{f(x)\}$.
For an open set $V$, the set $\{x:\Phi(x)\cap V\ne\emptyset\}$ equals $f^{-1}(V)$.
So $\Phi$ is lower hemicontinuous exactly when every $f^{-1}(V)$ is open.
That is the definition of a [continuous function](c:continuous-function).
links.why: It shows lower hemicontinuity as continuity extended to set-valued maps, so the open-preimage idea carries over.

reminder: The $L^p$ norm of a function is the $p$-th root of the integral of its absolute value to the power $p$.
definition: For a [measure space](c:measure-space) $(X,\mu)$ and $1\le p<\infty$, the $L^p$ norm of a [measurable function](c:measurable-function) $f$ is $\|f\|_p=\big(\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\big)^{1/p}$, the $p$-th root of an [integral](c:integral). For $p=\infty$, $\|f\|_\infty$ is the [essential supremum](c:essential-supremum) of $|f|$.
examples: On $[0,1]$ with Lebesgue measure, $\|x\|_2=\big(\int_0^1x^2\,dx\big)^{1/2}=1/\sqrt3$.
With counting measure on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ the $L^p$ norm is $\|x\|_p=(\sum_i|x_i|^p)^{1/p}$, the usual $\ell^p$ norm on $\mathbb R^n$.
$\|f\|_\infty$ is the least number $M$ with $|f|\le M$ almost everywhere.
Non-example: for $0<p<1$ the same formula fails the triangle inequality, so it is not a norm.

steps: Identify functions that agree almost everywhere, so that $\|f\|_p=0$ forces $f=0$.
Homogeneity $\|cf\|_p=|c|\,\|f\|_p$ follows by pulling $|c|^p$ out of the integral.
The triangle inequality $\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p$ is Minkowski's inequality, which needs $p\ge1$.
So $\|\cdot\|_p$ is a [norm](c:norm) on the space of classes with finite $L^p$ norm.
links.why: It shows that $L^p$ spaces are normed spaces, so every result about norms applies to them.

reminder: Lubin-Tate theory describes the universal deformation of a [formal group](c:formal-group) of finite height over a perfect field of characteristic $p$.
definition: Let $\Gamma$ be a [formal group](c:formal-group) of finite [height](c:height-of-a-formal-group) $n$ over a [perfect field](c:perfect-field) $k$ of characteristic $p$. Lubin-Tate theory shows that the deformations of $\Gamma$ to [complete local rings](c:complete-local-ring) with residue field $k$ have a universal deformation over the ring $W(k)[[u_1,\dots,u_{n-1}]]$, where $W(k)$ is the ring of Witt vectors; this ring is the degree-zero coefficient ring of [Morava E-theory](c:morava-e-theory).
examples: For height $n=1$ there are no parameters $u_i$, so the ring is $W(k)$.
For $n=2$ the ring is $W(k)[[u_1]]$, and it governs the deformations of the formal group of a [supersingular elliptic curve](c:supersingular-elliptic-curve).
The Goerss-Hopkins-Miller theorem gives an action of the automorphisms of $\Gamma$ on Morava E-theory, whose coefficient ring comes from this deformation ring.
Non-example: the additive formal group over $\mathbb F_p$ has infinite height, so the finite-height theory does not apply to it.

reminder: An M/M/1 queue has Poisson arrivals, exponential service times and a single server.
definition: An M/M/1 queue has one server and an unlimited waiting room, and it serves customers in order of arrival. Arrivals form a [Poisson process](c:poisson-process) of rate $\lambda$, and service times are independent and exponentially distributed with rate $\mu$, so the number of customers in the system is a continuous-time [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) that jumps up at rate $\lambda$ and down at rate $\mu$ when the system is not empty.
examples: Customers reach a single counter at rate $\lambda=2$ per minute and each service lasts on average $1/\mu=1/3$ minute.
If $\rho=\lambda/\mu<1$, the queue length has the stationary distribution $\pi_n=(1-\rho)\rho^n$.
Burke's theorem: in equilibrium the departures from an M/M/1 queue form a Poisson process of rate $\lambda$.
Non-example: an M/D/1 queue has constant service times, so its queue length alone is not a Markov chain.

reminder: Majority rule picks the alternative that more voters prefer, and declares a tie when the two counts are equal.
definition: Majority rule is the [social choice function](c:social-choice-function) for two alternatives that sends the votes $x_1,\dots,x_n\in\{-1,0,1\}$ of $n$ voters to $\operatorname{sign}(x_1+\dots+x_n)$, where the value $0$ is a tie. By May's theorem it is the only [voting system](c:voting-system) for two alternatives that is anonymous, neutral and positively responsive.
examples: With $5$ voters and votes $+,+,-,-,+$ the sum is $+1$, so the first alternative wins.
With $4$ voters split $2$ to $2$ the sum is $0$, so the outcome is a tie.
A committee that adopts a motion when more members vote for it than against it uses majority rule.
Non-example: a rule that needs two thirds of the votes is not majority rule, because it treats the two alternatives differently.

reminder: The Malliavin derivative differentiates a [random variable](c:random-variable) with respect to the underlying Gaussian noise.
definition: Let $W$ be an isonormal [Gaussian process](c:gaussian-process) on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$. For a smooth cylindrical [random variable](c:random-variable) $F=f(W(h_1),\dots,W(h_n))$, the Malliavin derivative is the $H$-valued random variable $DF=\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_if(W(h_1),\dots,W(h_n))\,h_i$, built from the [partial derivatives](c:partial-derivative) of $f$. It extends by closure to a domain $\mathbb D^{1,2}\subseteq L^2(\Omega)$.
examples: $D\,W(h)=h$ for every $h\in H$.
For Brownian motion $B$, $D_tB_s=\mathbf 1_{[0,s]}(t)$.
Non-example: $F=\mathbf 1_{\{B_1>0\}}$ is outside the domain $\mathbb D^{1,2}$, because it has a jump, so $DF$ does not exist as a random element of $H$.

reminder: The derivative of a smooth map between manifolds at a point is a linear map between the tangent spaces.
definition: For a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) $f:M\to N$ of [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold) and a point $p\in M$, the derivative $df_p$ is the [linear map](c:linear-map) $T_pM\to T_{f(p)}N$ between [tangent spaces](c:tangent-space) given by $df_p(\gamma'(0))=(f\circ\gamma)'(0)$ for every smooth curve $\gamma$ through $p$. In charts it is the [Jacobian matrix](c:jacobian-matrix) of $f$.
examples: For $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ the derivative $df_p$ is the usual Jacobian matrix $Df(p)$.
For a function $f:M\to\mathbb R$ the derivative $df_p$ is a linear functional on $T_pM$.
For the inclusion $i:S^2\to\mathbb R^3$ the derivative $di_p$ is injective, and its image is the plane tangent to the sphere at $p$.
Non-example: $x\mapsto|x|$ on $\mathbb R$ is not smooth at $0$, so it has no derivative $df_0$ there.

steps: Take open sets $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $V\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ as manifolds, with the identity charts.
Then $T_pU=\mathbb R^n$ and $T_{f(p)}V=\mathbb R^m$.
For a curve $\gamma$ through $p$ the chain rule gives $(f\circ\gamma)'(0)=Df(p)\,\gamma'(0)$.
So $df_p$ equals the ordinary [derivative](c:derivative) $Df(p)$.
links.why: It shows that the manifold derivative is the ordinary derivative made independent of coordinates.

reminder: A marginal distribution is the distribution of some of the variables, with the other variables summed or integrated out.
definition: Let $(X,Y)$ be a pair of [random variables](c:random-variable) with joint [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) $P$. The marginal distribution of $X$ is $P_X(A)=P\big((X,Y)\in A\times\mathcal Y\big)$, where $\mathcal Y$ is the set of values of $Y$; it is the [pushforward measure](c:pushforward-measure) of $P$ under the projection $(x,y)\mapsto x$. If $P$ has a [probability density function](c:probability-density-function) $f(x,y)$, then $X$ has the density $f_X(x)=\int f(x,y)\,dy$.
examples: For a discrete pair with joint table $p(x,y)$, the marginal is $p_X(x)=\sum_yp(x,y)$, the row sums.
If $(X,Y)$ is uniform on the unit square, the marginal distribution of $X$ is uniform on $[0,1]$.
A copula is a joint distribution on $[0,1]^2$ whose two marginal distributions are uniform; Sklar's theorem joins any given marginals through a copula.
Non-example: the conditional distribution of $X$ given $Y=y$ is not a marginal distribution, because it depends on $y$.

steps: Take a probability measure $P$ on a product space $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$.
Let $\pi:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathcal X$ be the projection $(x,y)\mapsto x$.
The [pushforward measure](c:pushforward-measure) is $\pi_*P(A)=P(\pi^{-1}(A))=P(A\times\mathcal Y)$.
This is the marginal distribution of $X$.
links.why: It shows that taking a marginal is pushing a measure forward along a projection, so pushforward rules apply.

reminder: The matrix exponential of a square matrix $A$ is the sum of the series $\sum_k A^k/k!$.
definition: For a square [matrix](c:matrix) $A$ over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, the matrix exponential is $e^A=\sum_{k=0}^\infty A^k/k!$, the [power series](c:power-series) of the [exponential function](c:exponential-function) evaluated at $A$. The series always converges, and $e^A$ is invertible with inverse $e^{-A}$.
examples: $e^0=I$, and for a diagonal matrix $e^{\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\dots,a_n)}=\operatorname{diag}(e^{a_1},\dots,e^{a_n})$.
For $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&-t\\t&0\end{pmatrix}$ the matrix $e^A$ is the rotation of the plane by the angle $t$.
The solution of $\dot x=Ax$ with $x(0)=x_0$ is $x(t)=e^{tA}x_0$, and the Magnus expansion extends this to a time-dependent matrix $A(t)$.

Non-example: the entrywise exponential is not the matrix exponential; for $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ we get $e^A=I+A$, which has a zero in the lower left entry, while the entrywise exponential has $e^0=1$ there.

steps: Take a $1\times1$ matrix $A=(a)$ with $a$ a real or complex number.
Its powers are $A^k=(a^k)$.
So the series $\sum_kA^k/k!$ is the matrix $(\sum_ka^k/k!)=(e^a)$.
Thus the matrix exponential of a $1\times1$ matrix is the scalar [exponential function](c:exponential-function).
links.why: It shows that the matrix exponential extends the scalar exponential, with the same series.

steps: Take the [general linear group](c:general-linear-group) $GL_n(\mathbb R)$, whose Lie algebra is the space of all real $n\times n$ matrices.
Its one-parameter subgroups are the curves $t\mapsto e^{tA}$, which solve $\dot g=gA$ with $g(0)=I$.
The exponential map sends $A$ to the value of that curve at $t=1$.
That value is $e^A$, so the exponential map of $GL_n$ is the matrix exponential.
links.why: It shows the matrix exponential as the exponential map of the matrix Lie group $GL_n$.

reminder: A matrix norm is a [norm](c:norm) on the space of matrices, usually with $\|AB\|\le\|A\|\,\|B\|$.
definition: A matrix norm is a [norm](c:norm) $\|\cdot\|$ on the [vector space](c:vector-space) of $m\times n$ [matrices](c:matrix): $\|A\|\ge0$ with equality only for $A=0$, $\|cA\|=|c|\,\|A\|$, and $\|A+B\|\le\|A\|+\|B\|$. For square matrices one usually also asks that it be submultiplicative, $\|AB\|\le\|A\|\,\|B\|$.
examples: The Frobenius norm $\|A\|_F=\sqrt{\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^2}$ is a submultiplicative matrix norm.
The operator norm $\|A\|=\sup_{\|x\|=1}\|Ax\|$ induced by a vector norm is submultiplicative, and the Bauer-Fike theorem is stated for such norms.
The max-entry norm $\max_{i,j}|a_{ij}|$ is a norm on the space of matrices but is not submultiplicative: for the $2\times2$ matrix $J$ of all ones, $\|J^2\|=2>1=\|J\|^2$.
Non-example: the absolute value of the determinant is not a matrix norm, because it is zero for non-zero singular matrices and $|\det(2A)|=2^n|\det A|$ is not $2|\det A|$.

steps: A [norm](c:norm) on a vector space has positivity, homogeneity and the triangle inequality.
Take the vector space of $n\times n$ matrices over a field $k$.
Any norm on this space is a matrix norm in the weak sense.
Add submultiplicativity $\|AB\|\le\|A\|\,\|B\|$ to get the usual definition.
links.why: It shows what is special about a matrix norm: the space has a product, and the norm is compatible with it.

reminder: An element $x$ of a dg Lie algebra solves the Maurer-Cartan equation when $dx+\tfrac12[x,x]=0$.
definition: Let $(\mathfrak g,[-,-],d)$ be a [differential graded Lie algebra](c:differential-graded-lie-algebra) with the differential $d$ of degree $1$. A Maurer-Cartan element is an element $x\in\mathfrak g^1$ with $dx+\tfrac12[x,x]=0$. In homological grading the element has degree $-1$ and the equation reads $\partial x+\tfrac12[x,x]=0$.
examples: In the dg Lie algebra of [Lie algebra-valued forms](c:lie-algebra-valued-form), a $1$-form $A$ solves the equation exactly when $dA+\tfrac12[A\wedge A]=0$, which means that $d+A$ is a [flat connection](c:flat-connection).
The [Maurer-Cartan form](c:maurer-cartan-form) $\theta=g^{-1}dg$ on a Lie group satisfies $d\theta+\tfrac12[\theta\wedge\theta]=0$.
In an abelian dg Lie algebra the bracket is zero, and the equation says only $dx=0$.

Non-example: on $\mathbb R^2$ take $A=a\,dx+b\,dy$ with constants $a,b\in\mathfrak g$ and $[a,b]\ne0$; then $dA=0$ but $\tfrac12[A\wedge A]=[a,b]\,dx\wedge dy\ne0$, so $A$ does not solve the equation.

steps: Take a trivial principal $G$-bundle on $M$ and a connection $d+A$ with $A$ a $\mathfrak g$-valued $1$-form.
The curvature of $d+A$ is $F=dA+\tfrac12[A\wedge A]$.
The connection is flat exactly when $F=0$.
That is the Maurer-Cartan equation in the dg Lie algebra of $\mathfrak g$-valued forms on $M$.
links.why: It shows that a flat connection is a Maurer-Cartan element in one particular dg Lie algebra.

steps: Take a dg coalgebra $C$ and a dg algebra $A$.
The graded linear maps $\operatorname{Hom}(C,A)$ form a dg Lie algebra with the convolution bracket.
A [twisting cochain](c:twisting-cochain) is a degree $1$ map $\tau$ with $d\tau+\tau\star\tau=0$.
Since $[\tau,\tau]=2\,\tau\star\tau$ for odd $\tau$, this is the Maurer-Cartan equation in that dg Lie algebra.
links.why: It shows that twisting cochains are Maurer-Cartan elements of a convolution dg Lie algebra.

reminder: The maximal ideal space of a commutative [Banach algebra](c:banach-algebra) is its set of maximal ideals with the Gelfand topology.
definition: Let $A$ be a commutative unital [Banach algebra](c:banach-algebra) over $\mathbb C$. Its maximal ideal space $M(A)$ is the set of [maximal ideals](c:maximal-ideal) of $A$, which correspond to the nonzero algebra homomorphisms $\varphi:A\to\mathbb C$ through $\ker\varphi$, with the [weak-star topology](c:weak-star-topology) from the dual of $A$; in this topology it is a [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space).
examples: For $A=C(K)$ with $K$ compact Hausdorff, $M(A)=K$, where a point corresponds to the ideal of functions that vanish there.
For the disc algebra of functions continuous on the closed unit disc and holomorphic inside, $M(A)$ is the closed [unit disc](c:unit-disc).
For $A=H^\infty$ of the open unit disc, $M(A)$ contains the open disc as a subset, and the Corona theorem says that this subset is dense.
Non-example: the prime spectrum of $C[0,1]$ is not its maximal ideal space, because it also has prime ideals that are not maximal.

reminder: The mean squared error of an estimator is the expected squared difference between the estimator and the true value.
definition: For an estimator $\hat\theta$, a [statistic](c:statistic) used to estimate a parameter $\theta$, the mean squared error is $\operatorname{MSE}(\hat\theta)=\mathbb E[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2]$, an [expected value](c:expected-value). It equals the [variance](c:variance) of $\hat\theta$ plus the squared bias $(\mathbb E\hat\theta-\theta)^2$.
examples: For the sample mean $\bar X$ of $n$ independent observations with variance $\sigma^2$, the mean squared error is $\sigma^2/n$.
The constant estimator $\hat\theta=0$ has mean squared error $\theta^2$, all of it from bias.
By the Rao-Blackwell theorem, replacing an estimator by its conditional expectation given a sufficient statistic does not increase the mean squared error.
Non-example: the mean absolute error $\mathbb E|\hat\theta-\theta|$ is not the mean squared error, because it uses the absolute value instead of the square.

reminder: A function has the mean value property when its value at each point equals its average over spheres centered at that point.
definition: Let $u$ be a [continuous function](c:continuous-function) on an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. It has the mean value property if $u(x)$ equals the average of $u$ over the [sphere](c:sphere) of radius $r$ centered at $x$, for every closed [ball](c:ball) $\overline{B_r(x)}\subset\Omega$. The solid version uses averages over the ball instead of the sphere.
examples: Every [harmonic function](c:harmonic-function) has the mean value property, and a continuous function with the property is harmonic.
$u(x,y)=x^2-y^2$ is harmonic, so $u(0,0)=0$ equals its average over each circle around the origin.
The Poisson integral formula gives a harmonic function on a disc from its boundary values, and at the center it reduces to the mean value property.
Non-example: $u(x)=x^2$ on $\mathbb R$ fails the property, because the average over the two points $x\pm r$ is $x^2+r^2\ne x^2$.

reminder: A measurable embedding is an injective measurable map that sends measurable sets to measurable sets.
definition: A map $f:\alpha\to\beta$ between [measurable spaces](c:measurable-space) is a measurable embedding if it is an [injection](c:injection), is a [measurable function](c:measurable-function), and sends every measurable set of $\alpha$ to a measurable set of $\beta$. It is then a measurable isomorphism of $\alpha$ onto its image, which is a measurable subset of $\beta$.
examples: The inclusion of a measurable subset $A\subseteq X$ into $X$ is a measurable embedding.
Every injective Borel map between standard Borel spaces is a measurable embedding, by the Lusin-Souslin theorem.
Every measurable bijection with a measurable inverse is a measurable embedding.

Non-example: the identity map from $\mathbb R$ with the power-set sigma-algebra to $\mathbb R$ with the Borel sigma-algebra is injective and measurable, but a non-Borel set is measurable in the domain and its image is not measurable.

steps: A [measurable function](c:measurable-function) pulls measurable sets of the target back to measurable sets of the source.
Take such a function that is also injective.
Add the condition that images of measurable sets are measurable, which is the same as pulling back along the inverse on the image.
Then the function is a measurable embedding.
links.why: It shows what an embedding adds to a measurable map: injectivity and measurable images.

reminder: A measure algebra is the Boolean algebra of measurable sets modulo null sets, with the measure induced on it.
definition: For a [measure space](c:measure-space) $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, call $A,B\in\Sigma$ equivalent if their symmetric difference is a [null set](c:null-set). The measure algebra is the quotient of the [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) $\Sigma$ by this relation, a [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) with operations induced by union, intersection and complement, together with the measure $\mu$, which is well defined on the classes.
examples: For Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$ the sets $[0,\tfrac12]$ and $[0,\tfrac12)$ give the same element of the measure algebra.
By Maharam's theorem a homogeneous measure algebra is determined, up to isomorphism, by its total measure and a cardinal number, its Maharam type.
For a finite set with a probability measure that gives every point positive weight, the measure algebra is the power set.
Non-example: the Borel sigma-algebra itself is not a measure algebra, because $\{0\}$ and $\emptyset$ are different sets in it, while in the measure algebra of $[0,1]$ they are identified.

steps: Start with the sigma-algebra $\Sigma$, which is a [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) under union, intersection and complement.
The null sets form a sigma-ideal $\mathcal N$, so the quotient $\Sigma/\mathcal N$ is again a Boolean algebra.
The measure vanishes on $\mathcal N$, so it descends to the quotient and is strictly positive there.
The result is a Boolean algebra with a strictly positive measure.
links.why: It shows that a measure algebra is a Boolean algebra with a strictly positive measure, so order and lattice facts apply.

reminder: A set has measure zero when countably many boxes of arbitrarily small total volume cover it.
definition: A subset $A\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ has Lebesgue measure zero if for every $\varepsilon>0$ some [countable](c:countable-set) family of boxes covers $A$ with total volume less than $\varepsilon$; equivalently $\lambda(A)=0$ for [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) $\lambda$. In a [measure space](c:measure-space) $(X,\mu)$ a set $A$ has measure zero when $\mu(A)=0$, and a subset of a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) has measure zero when its image in every chart does.
examples: Every countable subset of $\mathbb R$, such as $\mathbb Q$, has measure zero.
The Cantor set has measure zero, although it is uncountable.
Sard's theorem says that the set of critical values of a smooth map has measure zero.
Non-example: an interval $[a,b]$ with $a<b$ has measure $b-a>0$, so it does not have measure zero.

steps: A [null set](c:null-set) of a measure space $(X,\mu)$ is a set $N$ with $\mu(N)=0$.
Take $X=\mathbb R^n$ and let $\mu$ be Lebesgue measure.
A subset has Lebesgue measure zero exactly when it is such a null set, and the box covers give an equivalent test.
links.why: It shows that measure zero in $\mathbb R^n$ is the null set of Lebesgue measure, so general null set facts apply.

reminder: The Mellin transform of $f$ is the integral of $f(x)\,x^{s-1}$ over $x$ from zero to infinity.
definition: For a [function](c:function) $f:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb C$, the Mellin transform is $\mathcal Mf(s)=\int_0^\infty f(x)\,x^{s-1}\,dx$, defined for the [complex numbers](c:complex-number) $s$ at which the [integral](c:integral) converges absolutely. With $x=e^{-t}$ it becomes the two-sided Laplace transform of $f(e^{-t})$.
examples: For $f(x)=e^{-x}$ we get $\mathcal Mf(s)=\Gamma(s)$ for $\operatorname{Re}s>0$, the [Gamma function](c:gamma-function).
For the indicator function $f=\mathbf 1_{(0,1)}$ we get $\mathcal Mf(s)=1/s$ for $\operatorname{Re}s>0$.

For $\psi(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-\pi n^2x}$ we get $\mathcal M\psi(s/2)=\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)$ for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$, which gives the [functional equation](c:functional-equation) of the zeta function.
Non-example: $f(x)=x$ has no Mellin transform, because $\int_0^\infty x^{s}\,dx$ diverges for every $s$.

steps: An [integral transform](c:integral-transform) sends $f$ to $Tf(s)=\int K(s,x)\,f(x)\,dx$ for a kernel $K$.
Take the interval $(0,\infty)$ for $x$ and the kernel $K(s,x)=x^{s-1}$.
Then $Tf(s)=\int_0^\infty f(x)\,x^{s-1}\,dx$ is the Mellin transform.
links.why: It shows the Mellin transform as the integral transform with a power kernel.

reminder: The minimum excludant of a set of natural numbers is the smallest natural number that is not in the set.
definition: For a [set](c:set) $S$ of [natural numbers](c:natural-number) with $S\ne\mathbb N$, $\operatorname{mex}(S)$ is the least element of $\mathbb N\setminus S$, which exists because $\mathbb N$ is [well-ordered](c:well-order).
examples: $\operatorname{mex}\{0,1,3\}=2$.
$\operatorname{mex}(\emptyset)=0$ and $\operatorname{mex}\{1,2\}=0$.
In the Sprague-Grundy theorem the Grundy value of a game position is the mex of the Grundy values of the positions that a move can reach.
Non-example: the mex of $\mathbb N$ itself is not defined as a natural number, because every natural number is in the set.

reminder: Milnor K-theory of a field is the graded ring generated by symbols of units with the Steinberg relation.
definition: For a [field](c:field) $F$, the Milnor K-theory ring $K^M_*(F)$ is the quotient of the [tensor algebra](c:tensor-algebra) over $\mathbb Z$ of the [group of units](c:group-of-units) $F^\times$ by the two-sided ideal generated by the elements $a\otimes(1-a)$ with $a\ne0,1$. It is a [graded ring](c:graded-ring), and the class of $a_1\otimes\dots\otimes a_n$ in degree $n$ is the symbol $\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}$.
examples: $K^M_0(F)=\mathbb Z$ and $K^M_1(F)=F^\times$.
By Matsumoto's theorem $K^M_2(F)$ is generated by symbols $\{a,b\}$ that are multiplicative in each entry with $\{a,1-a\}=0$, and it equals Quillen's $K_2(F)$.
For a finite field $\mathbb F_q$ we have $K^M_n(\mathbb F_q)=0$ for $n\ge2$.
Non-example: Quillen's [algebraic K-theory](c:algebraic-k-theory) is not Milnor K-theory; for a finite field $K_3(\mathbb F_q)\cong\mathbb Z/(q^2-1)$ is non-zero, while $K^M_3(\mathbb F_q)=0$.

reminder: A minimal model of a differential graded algebra is a quasi-isomorphic algebra whose differential has no linear part.
definition: A minimal model of a [differential graded algebra](c:differential-graded-algebra) $A$ is an algebra $M$ with a [quasi-isomorphism](c:quasi-isomorphism) $M\to A$ whose differential has no linear part. For a [Sullivan model](c:sullivan-model), $M=(\Lambda V,d)$ is free graded-commutative with $d(V)\subseteq\Lambda^{\ge2}V$. In the $A_\infty$ version, $M$ is the homology of $A$ with an [A-infinity algebra](c:a-infinity-algebra) structure whose first operation $m_1$ is zero.
examples: The minimal Sullivan model of the $3$-sphere $S^3$ is $(\Lambda(x),0)$ with $x$ of degree $3$.
The minimal Sullivan model of $S^2$ is $\Lambda(x,y)$ with $|x|=2$, $|y|=3$ and $dy=x^2$.
Kadeishvili's theorem: every differential graded algebra over a field has a minimal $A_\infty$ model on its homology.
Non-example: $\Lambda(x,y)$ with $|x|=1$, $|y|=2$ and $dy=x$ is quasi-isomorphic to the base field but is not minimal, because $dy=x$ has a linear part.

reminder: The minmax payoff of a player is the lowest payoff that the other players can hold that player to.
definition: In a finite game with payoff function $u_i$ for player $i$, the minmax payoff of $i$ is $\underline v_i=\min_{\alpha_{-i}}\max_{a_i}u_i(a_i,\alpha_{-i})$, where $\alpha_{-i}$ ranges over [mixed strategy](c:mixed-strategy) profiles of the other players and $a_i$ over the actions of $i$. In a [repeated game](c:repeated-game), the payoff of player $i$ in a [Nash equilibrium](c:nash-equilibrium) is never below $\underline v_i$.
examples: In the Prisoner's Dilemma with payoffs $3,0,5,1$ for (cooperate, cooperate), (cooperate, defect), (defect, cooperate), (defect, defect), the minmax payoff of each player is $1$.
In matching pennies with payoffs $\pm1$ the minmax payoff of each player is $0$, reached when the other player mixes with probability $\tfrac12$.
The folk theorem says that, for patient players in a repeated game, every feasible payoff vector that gives each player more than the minmax payoff is an equilibrium payoff.
Non-example: in matching pennies the value $1$, found when the other player uses only pure actions, is not the minmax payoff, because mixing holds the player to $0$.

reminder: A mixture of distributions is a weighted average of distributions, where the weights form a probability distribution.
definition: Let $P_\theta$ be [probability measures](c:probability-measure) indexed by a parameter $\theta$, and let $\pi$ be a probability measure on the parameters. The mixture is the measure $P(A)=\int P_\theta(A)\,d\pi(\theta)$, and for finitely many components it is $P=\sum_iw_iP_i$ with $w_i\ge0$ and $\sum_iw_i=1$.
examples: Pick a coin with equal probability from a fair coin and a coin with heads probability $0.9$; the chance of heads is the mixture $\tfrac12(0.5)+\tfrac12(0.9)=0.7$.
The mixture $\tfrac12N(0,1)+\tfrac12N(5,1)$ of two normal distributions has two modes.
By de Finetti's theorem, an infinite exchangeable sequence of $0$-$1$ variables is a mixture of independent identically distributed Bernoulli sequences.
Non-example: the distribution of a sum $X+Y$ of independent variables is the convolution of their distributions, not a mixture of them.

reminder: A modular curve is a quotient of the upper half plane by a congruence subgroup, and it parametrizes elliptic curves with level structure.
definition: A modular curve is a [moduli space](c:moduli-space) of [elliptic curves](c:elliptic-curve) over $\mathbb C$ with [level structure](c:level-structure-on-an-elliptic-curve) of some level $N$. Concretely, it is the quotient $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H$ of the [upper half plane](c:upper-half-plane) by a [congruence subgroup](c:congruence-subgroup) $\Gamma\subseteq SL_2(\mathbb Z)$ such as $\Gamma_0(N)$ or $\Gamma(N)$, usually with finitely many cusps added to make it compact.
examples: $Y(1)=SL_2(\mathbb Z)\backslash\mathbb H$ is the moduli space of all elliptic curves over $\mathbb C$, and the $j$-invariant identifies it with $\mathbb C$.
$X_0(11)$ is a compact modular curve of genus $1$.
A point of $Y_1(N)$ is an elliptic curve with a point of order $N$, and Mazur's torsion theorem is a statement about rational points of these curves.
Non-example: the upper half plane $\mathbb H$ itself is not a modular curve, because every congruence subgroup has finite index in $SL_2(\mathbb Z)$ and so is not trivial.

steps: A [moduli space](c:moduli-space) has one point for each isomorphism class of some kind of object.
Take the objects to be pairs $(E,\alpha)$ of an elliptic curve $E$ over $\mathbb C$ and a level-$N$ structure $\alpha$.
Each $E$ is $\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\tau\mathbb Z)$ for some $\tau\in\mathbb H$, and $\tau,\tau'$ give isomorphic pairs when $\tau'=\gamma\tau$ for some $\gamma$ in the congruence subgroup.
So the moduli space is the quotient $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H$.
links.why: It shows why the quotient of the upper half plane is a moduli space, so a point of it is an elliptic curve with extra structure.

steps: Take the group $GL_2$ over $\mathbb Q$, whose symmetric domain is the union $\mathbb H^{\pm}$ of the upper and lower half planes.
Choose a compact open subgroup $K\subseteq GL_2(\mathbb A_f)$ of level $N$.
The double coset space of $\mathbb H^{\pm}\times GL_2(\mathbb A_f)$ by $GL_2(\mathbb Q)$ and $K$ is a [Shimura variety](c:shimura-variety) of dimension one.
Its connected components are the modular curves $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H$.
links.why: It shows that modular curves are the one-dimensional Shimura varieties, which places them in the general theory.
